title: Redox Reactions
lines: Redox questions look different on the surface but always ask one of four things: which element changes oxidation state, which substance is the oxidising or reducing agent, how many electrons move, or what happens at an electrode. Master oxidation numbers and the rest follows.
## Oxidation numbers

- Rules in order: an element alone is 0 (Fe, O₂, Cl₂). In compounds F is always −1; group 1 metals +1; group 2 metals +2; Al +3; H is +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH); O is −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂ and Na₂O₂).
- The sum is 0 for a neutral compound and equals the charge for an ion.
> Example: Find the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄, of S in Na₂S₂O₃ and of N in NH₄⁺.
> KMnO₄: 1 + x − 8 = 0, so Mn = +7. Na₂S₂O₃: 2 + 2x − 6 = 0, so S = +2 (average). NH₄⁺: x + 4 = +1, so N = −3.
- Common ranges: N from −3 (NH₃) to +5 (HNO₃); S from −2 (H₂S) to +6 (H₂SO₄); Cl from −1 (HCl) to +7 (HClO₄); Mn from +2 (Mn²⁺) to +7 (MnO₄⁻).
## Oxidation and reduction
- Oxidation is loss of electrons, so the oxidation number rises. Reduction is gain of electrons, so it falls. Memory trick: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
- A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes. Oxidation and reduction always happen together, and electrons lost = electrons gained.

- The oxidising agent is reduced (it takes electrons); the reducing agent is oxidised (it gives electrons). The product of reduction is the reduced product; the product of oxidation is the oxidised product.
! Memory trick: "The agent does to others what is done to itself in reverse." An oxidising agent oxidises something else, and is itself reduced.
> Example: In MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc.) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat), identify the agents and the moles of HCl oxidised per mole MnO₂.
> Mn goes from +4 to +2 (reduced), so MnO₂ is the oxidising agent. Cl goes from −1 to 0 in Cl₂, so HCl is the reducing agent.
> Only 2 of the 4 Cl atoms become Cl₂, so 2 mol HCl is oxidised; the other 2 mol acts as an acid in MnCl₂.
! Trap: in this reaction dilute HCl does not work; as the acid is used up and becomes dilute the reaction stops, so the Cl₂ formed is less than the HCl amount predicts.
## Strength of oxidising and reducing agents
- In a reaction that goes, oxidising agent > oxidised product in oxidising power, and reducing agent > reduced product in reducing power.
> Example: Given 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and Cl₂ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻, order the oxidising agents.
> From the first: Fe³⁺ > I₂. From the second: Cl₂ > Fe³⁺. So Cl₂ > Fe³⁺ > I₂. Reducing power runs the other way: I⁻ > Fe²⁺ > Cl⁻.
- Common strong oxidising agents: F₂, Cl₂, O₂, concentrated H₂SO₄, HNO₃, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, Fe³⁺, HClO, H₂O₂, Na₂O₂. Common reducing agents: active metals, H₂, C, CO, H₂S, S²⁻, I⁻, SO₂, SO₃²⁻, Fe²⁺.
- An element in its highest state can only be oxidising (S in H₂SO₄, N in HNO₃); in its lowest state only reducing (S²⁻, I⁻); in a middle state it can be either (SO₂, Fe²⁺, H₂O₂, Cl₂).

- Priority rule: when one oxidising agent meets several reducing agents, the strongest reducing agent reacts first. Cl₂ added to FeBr₂ oxidises Fe²⁺ before Br⁻; Cl₂ added to FeI₂ oxidises I⁻ before Fe²⁺.
## Electron transfer and counting
- Electrons transferred = (change in oxidation number per atom) × (number of atoms that change).
> Example: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. How many electrons are transferred per mole of O₂ formed?
> O goes from −2 to 0: 2 electrons per O atom, 4 per O₂ molecule. So 4 mol electrons per mol O₂ (and 12 for the whole equation as written).
> Example: In Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, how many electrons move per mole of Cl₂?
> One Cl goes 0 → −1, the other 0 → +1, so 1 mol electrons per mol Cl₂. Cl₂ is both oxidising and reducing agent (disproportionation).
- Comproportionation: two states meet in the middle, e.g. 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O. Oxidised product and reduced product are both S, in a ratio 2 : 1.
- A middle state never jumps over another: in KClO₃ + 6HCl → KCl + 3Cl₂ + 3H₂O, the +5 Cl goes to 0, not to −1, so only 5 electrons are transferred, and Cl₂ is both the oxidised and reduced product.
! Trap: in the last reaction the KCl chlorine comes from HCl, not from KClO₃. That is why the electrons transferred are 5, not 6.
## Balancing redox equations

- Step 1: mark the oxidation numbers that change. Step 2: find the electrons lost and gained per formula. Step 3: use the lowest common multiple to equalise electrons. Step 4: balance other atoms by inspection, then H and O (with H⁺/H₂O in acid or OH⁻/H₂O in base). Step 5: check charge for ionic equations.
> Example: Balance MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O.
> Mn +7 → +2 gains 5; Fe +2 → +3 loses 1. So 1 MnO₄⁻ to 5 Fe²⁺.
> Oxygen: 4 O gives 4H₂O, needing 8H⁺. MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.
> Charge check: left −1 + 10 + 8 = +17; right +2 + 15 = +17. Balanced.
> Example: Balance Cu + HNO₃(dilute) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO + H₂O.
> Cu loses 2; N (+5 → +2) gains 3. LCM 6: 3Cu and 2NO. Then 6 nitrate in 3Cu(NO₃)₂ plus 2 N in NO = 8HNO₃, giving 4H₂O.
> 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO↑ + 4H₂O.
! Shortcut for calculations: you rarely need the full equation. Electron conservation alone answers questions like "how much KMnO₄ oxidises 0.5 mol Fe²⁺?": 0.5 mol electrons, so 0.1 mol MnO₄⁻.
## Galvanic (primary) cells

- A galvanic cell turns chemical energy into electrical energy using a spontaneous redox reaction. It needs two different electrodes (or a metal and an inert conductor), an electrolyte and a closed circuit.
- The negative electrode (anode) is where oxidation happens; it is usually the more active metal. The positive electrode (cathode) is where reduction happens.
- Electrons flow through the external wire from negative to positive. In the solution, cations move to the positive electrode and anions to the negative electrode.
- Zn–Cu cell in dilute H₂SO₄: negative Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; positive 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ (bubbles appear on the copper).
- Hydrogen fuel cell (acidic): negative 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; positive O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. In alkaline electrolyte: negative 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; positive O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
- Lead-acid battery discharge: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; both electrodes gain mass as PbSO₄ forms.

- Corrosion: iron rusts faster when in contact with a less active metal (Fe is the negative electrode). Electrochemical corrosion in neutral or weakly acidic water is oxygen-absorbing: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Protection: connect a more active metal (Zn, sacrificial anode) or connect to the negative terminal of a power supply.
! Trap: in an Mg–Al cell with NaOH electrolyte, Al is the negative electrode, because only Al reacts with NaOH. In an Fe–Cu cell with concentrated HNO₃, Cu is negative because Fe is passivated.
> Example: In a Zn–Cu–H₂SO₄ cell, 6.5 g of Zn dissolves. What volume of H₂ forms at STP?
> n(Zn) = 0.1 mol, 0.2 mol electrons, so 0.1 mol H₂ = 2.24 L.
## Electrolysis basics
- Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction. The anode joins the positive terminal (oxidation); the cathode joins the negative terminal (reduction).
- At an inert cathode (graphite or Pt) the most easily reduced cation gains electrons: Ag⁺ > Cu²⁺ > H⁺ > Na⁺ (active metal ions are not reduced from solution; water's H⁺ is).

- At an inert anode the most easily oxidised anion loses electrons: S²⁻ > I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > OH⁻ > sulfate and nitrate (these are never oxidised; water is). An active metal anode (Cu, Fe) dissolves itself.
- Examples: CuCl₂(aq) → Cu + Cl₂; brine 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ + Cl₂↑ (H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode); CuSO₄(aq): 2CuSO₄ + 2H₂O → 2Cu + O₂↑ + 2H₂SO₄.

- Electroplating: object to be plated is the cathode, plating metal is the anode, and the electrolyte contains its ions; the electrolyte concentration stays constant. Copper refining: impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode.
- Molten electrolysis extracts active metals: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na + Cl₂; 2Al₂O₃(l) → 4Al + 3O₂ (with cryolite). MgCl₂ (molten) gives Mg; AlCl₃ is not used because it is covalent.
> Example: Electrolysing CuSO₄ solution with inert electrodes deposits 6.4 g of copper. What volume of O₂ forms at STP?
> n(Cu) = 0.1 mol, 0.2 mol electrons. O₂ needs 4 electrons per molecule, so 0.05 mol = 1.12 L.

! Memory trick: "An Ox, Red Cat" (anode oxidation, reduction at cathode) works for both cell types. Only the signs differ: in a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in electrolysis the anode is positive.
